Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.

- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# process tow tank runs -> mean drag force for each run
#
# Handles both DAQ file formats (v2.1 comma-separated with "#" header, and the
# March 2026 semicolon format), picks the load cell calibration in effect on
# the run date, and flags runs whose zero drifted during the tow.
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import signal

RAW = "data/raw"
FS = 200.0  # Hz
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # s, carriage at rest before the tow
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # s, constant-speed part of the tow
POST_WINDOW = 1.0  # s, last part of the record, carriage at rest again
MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N = 0.05  # N, |post-run zero - pre-run tare| above this -> excluded

# Calibration in effect from each date (load cell remounted 2026-03-10)
CALIBRATIONS = [
    ("2025-09-30", "data/calibration/loadcell_2025-09.csv"),
    ("2026-03-10", "data/calibration/loadcell_2026-03.csv"),
]


def fit_calibration(path):
    """Linear fit of voltage vs applied force; returns slope (V/N) and its std error."""
    cal = pd.read_csv(path)
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * 9.81
    p, cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    return p[0], np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])


def calibration_for(date):
    valid = [c for c in CALIBRATIONS if c[0] <= date]
    return valid[-1][1]


def read_run(path):
    """Return time (s) and load cell voltage (V) for either DAQ file format."""
    with open(path) as f:
        first = f.readline()
    if first.startswith("#"):
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
        return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
    return d.t.values, d.V.values


def mean_uncertainty(x, f_dominant):
    """Standard error of the mean, treating each fluctuation cycle as one
    independent sample (the force is dominated by a periodic component)."""
    n_eff = max(len(x) / FS * f_dominant, 1.0)
    return x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_eff)


def dominant_frequency(x):
    """Frequency (Hz) of the largest peak in the force spectrum above 1 Hz."""
    # Whole steady window with zero padding: the window is only ~5 s long
    f, pxx = signal.periodogram(x - x.mean(), fs=FS, window="hann", nfft=2**15)
    mask = f > 1.0
    return f[mask][np.argmax(pxx[mask])]


log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
sens = {path: fit_calibration(path) for _, path in CALIBRATIONS}
for path, (s, s_err) in sens.items():
    print(f"{path}: sensitivity {s:.5f} +/- {s_err:.5f} V/N")

rows = []
for r in log.itertuples():
    cal_path = calibration_for(r.date)
    s, s_err = sens[cal_path]
    t, v = read_run(os.path.join(RAW, r.date, f"run_{r.run_id:03d}.csv"))
    tare = v[(t >= TARE_WINDOW[0]) & (t < TARE_WINDOW[1])].mean()
    post = v[t > t[-1] - POST_WINDOW].mean()
    F = (v - tare) / s
    Fs = F[(t > STEADY_WINDOW[0]) & (t < STEADY_WINDOW[1])]
    zero_drift = (post - tare) / s
    f_peak = dominant_frequency(Fs)
    rows.append({
        "run": r.run_id,
        "calibration": os.path.basename(cal_path),
        "sens_V_per_N": s,
        "sens_std_err": s_err,
        "F_mean": Fs.mean(),
        "F_std": Fs.std(ddof=1),
        "F_mean_unc": mean_uncertainty(Fs, f_peak),
        "f_peak_Hz": f_peak,
        "zero_drift_N": zero_drift,
        "excluded": abs(zero_drift) > MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N,
    })

out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
os.makedirs("processed", exist_ok=True)
out.to_csv("processed/forces.csv", index=False)
print(f"processed {len(out)} runs, excluded: {out.run[out.excluded].tolist()}")
# mean forces + run log -> Cd, Re, St per run, summary numbers, and the
# Cd/St vs Re figure and LaTeX table/macros used in the paper
import os

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

L = 0.60  # m, submerged length
TANK_W = 0.90  # m
TANK_H = 0.75  # m, water depth
G = 9.81
MASKELL_M = 2.5  # empirical blockage factor for the Maskell-type correction

# Fixed cylinder -> color/marker, ordered by diameter (validated palette)
STYLE = {
    "1in": ("#2a78d6", "o"),
    "1.5in": ("#eb6834", "s"),
    "2in": ("#1baf7a", "^"),
}
LABEL = {"1in": "$D$ = 25.4 mm", "1.5in": "$D$ = 38.1 mm", "2in": "$D$ = 50.8 mm"}


def water_density(T):
    """kg/m^3, Tanaka et al. (2001), T in deg C."""
    a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 = -3.983035, 301.797, 522528.9, 69.34881, 999.974950
    return a5 * (1 - (T + a1) ** 2 * (T + a2) / (a3 * (T + a4)))


def water_viscosity(T):
    """Pa s, Vogel-type correlation, T in deg C."""
    return 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (T + 273.15 - 140.0))


f = pd.read_csv("processed/forces.csv")
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
df = f.merge(log, left_on="run", right_on="run_id")

D = df.diameter_mm / 1000
U = df.speed_m_s
df["rho"] = water_density(df.water_temp_c)
df["nu"] = water_viscosity(df.water_temp_c) / df.rho
df["Re"] = U * D / df.nu
df["Re_20C"] = U * D / 1.004e-6  # as in the original notebook, for comparison
q_A = 0.5 * df.rho * U**2 * D * L
df["Cd"] = df.F_mean / q_A
# random (block-averaged) + calibration slope uncertainty, added in quadrature
df["Cd_unc"] = df.Cd * np.sqrt(
    (df.F_mean_unc / df.F_mean) ** 2 + (df.sens_std_err / df.sens_V_per_N) ** 2
)
# drag fluctuates at twice the shedding frequency
df["St"] = df.f_peak_Hz / 2 * D / U
df["Fr"] = U / np.sqrt(G * D)
df["LD"] = L / D
df["blockage"] = D * L / (TANK_W * TANK_H)
df["Cd_corr"] = df.Cd / (1 + MASKELL_M * df.Cd * df.blockage)

os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)
cols = ["run", "cylinder", "diameter_mm", "speed_m_s", "water_temp_c", "rho", "nu",
        "Re", "Fr", "F_mean", "F_mean_unc", "Cd", "Cd_unc", "Cd_corr", "St",
        "zero_drift_N", "excluded"]
df[cols].to_csv("results/cd.csv", index=False)

good = df[~df.excluded]
order = ["1in", "1.5in", "2in"]
summary = good.groupby("cylinder").agg(
    D=("diameter_mm", "first"), n=("run", "size"), Cd=("Cd", "mean"),
    Cd_sd=("Cd", "std"), Cd_corr=("Cd_corr", "mean"), St=("St", "mean"),
    blockage=("blockage", "first"), LD=("LD", "first"),
    Re_min=("Re", "min"), Re_max=("Re", "max"),
).loc[order]
summary.to_csv("results/summary.csv")
print(summary.round(4).to_string())

# Pooled linear trend of Cd with log10(Re)
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(np.log10(good.Re), good.Cd, 1)
re_shift = (df.Re_20C / df.Re - 1).agg(["min", "max"]) * 100
print(f"Cd trend: {slope:.3f} per decade of Re; Re(20C) overestimate "
      f"{re_shift['min']:.1f}-{re_shift['max']:.1f}%")

# --- Figure: Cd and St vs Re ---
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(4.5, 5.0), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]})
ax_cd, ax_st = axes
for cyl in order:
    g = good[good.cylinder == cyl]
    color, marker = STYLE[cyl]
    kw = dict(color=color, marker=marker, ms=5, mec="white", mew=0.8, ls="none")
    ax_cd.errorbar(g.Re, g.Cd, yerr=g.Cd_unc, ecolor=color, elinewidth=1,
                   capsize=0, label=LABEL[cyl], **kw)
    ax_st.plot(g.Re, g.St, **kw)
bad = df[df.excluded]
ax_cd.plot(bad.Re, bad.Cd, marker="^", ms=5, mfc="none", mec="0.5", ls="none",
           label="Excluded (zero drift)")
for r in bad.itertuples():
    ax_cd.annotate(f"run {r.run}", (r.Re, r.Cd), xytext=(6, 0),
                   textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=8, color="0.35")
ax_cd.set_ylabel("$C_D$")
handles, labels = ax_cd.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax_cd.legend(handles[1:] + handles[:1], labels[1:] + labels[:1], frameon=False,
             fontsize=8, ncol=2, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0))
ax_st.set_ylabel("St")
ax_st.set_ylim(0.15, 0.25)
ax_st.set_xscale("log")
ax_st.set_xlabel("Re")
ax_st.set_xticks([5e3, 1e4, 2e4, 5e4], ["5000", "10 000", "20 000", "50 000"])
ax_st.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(plt.NullFormatter())

fig.tight_layout()
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)

fig.savefig("figures/cd_st_vs_re.png", dpi=200)

# process tow tank runs -> mean drag force for each run
#
# Handles both DAQ file formats (v2.1 comma-separated with "#" header, and the
# March 2026 semicolon format), picks the load cell calibration in effect on
# the run date, and flags runs whose zero drifted during the tow.
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import signal

RAW = "data/raw"
FS = 200.0  # Hz
TARE_WINDOW = (0.0, 1.0)  # s, carriage at rest before the tow
STEADY_WINDOW = (3.0, 8.0)  # s, constant-speed part of the tow
POST_WINDOW = 1.0  # s, last part of the record, carriage at rest again
MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N = 0.05  # N, |post-run zero - pre-run tare| above this -> excluded

# Calibration in effect from each date (load cell remounted 2026-03-10)
CALIBRATIONS = [
    ("2025-09-30", "data/calibration/loadcell_2025-09.csv"),
    ("2026-03-10", "data/calibration/loadcell_2026-03.csv"),
]


def fit_calibration(path):
    """Linear fit of voltage vs applied force; returns slope (V/N) and its std error."""
    cal = pd.read_csv(path)
    force = cal.mass_g / 1000 * 9.81
    p, cov = np.polyfit(force, cal.voltage_V, 1, cov=True)
    return p[0], np.sqrt(cov[0, 0])


def calibration_for(date):
    valid = [c for c in CALIBRATIONS if c[0] <= date]
    return valid[-1][1]


def read_run(path):
    """Return time (s) and load cell voltage (V) for either DAQ file format."""
    with open(path) as f:
        first = f.readline()
    if first.startswith("#"):
        d = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
        return d.time_s.values, d.loadcell_V.values
    d = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";")
    return d.t.values, d.V.values


def mean_uncertainty(x, f_dominant):
    """Standard error of the mean, treating each fluctuation cycle as one
    independent sample (the force is dominated by a periodic component)."""
    n_eff = max(len(x) / FS * f_dominant, 1.0)
    return x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_eff)


def dominant_frequency(x):
    """Frequency (Hz) of the largest peak in the force spectrum above 1 Hz."""
    # Whole steady window with zero padding: the window is only ~5 s long
    f, pxx = signal.periodogram(x - x.mean(), fs=FS, window="hann", nfft=2**15)
    mask = f > 1.0
    return f[mask][np.argmax(pxx[mask])]


log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
sens = {path: fit_calibration(path) for _, path in CALIBRATIONS}
for path, (s, s_err) in sens.items():
    print(f"{path}: sensitivity {s:.5f} +/- {s_err:.5f} V/N")

rows = []
for r in log.itertuples():
    cal_path = calibration_for(r.date)
    s, s_err = sens[cal_path]
    t, v = read_run(os.path.join(RAW, r.date, f"run_{r.run_id:03d}.csv"))
    tare = v[(t >= TARE_WINDOW[0]) & (t < TARE_WINDOW[1])].mean()
    post = v[t > t[-1] - POST_WINDOW].mean()
    F = (v - tare) / s
    Fs = F[(t > STEADY_WINDOW[0]) & (t < STEADY_WINDOW[1])]
    zero_drift = (post - tare) / s
    f_peak = dominant_frequency(Fs)
    rows.append({
        "run": r.run_id,
        "calibration": os.path.basename(cal_path),
        "sens_V_per_N": s,
        "sens_std_err": s_err,
        "F_mean": Fs.mean(),
        "F_std": Fs.std(ddof=1),
        "F_mean_unc": mean_uncertainty(Fs, f_peak),
        "f_peak_Hz": f_peak,
        "zero_drift_N": zero_drift,
        "excluded": abs(zero_drift) > MAX_ZERO_DRIFT_N,
    })

out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
os.makedirs("processed", exist_ok=True)
out.to_csv("processed/forces.csv", index=False)
print(f"processed {len(out)} runs, excluded: {out.run[out.excluded].tolist()}")
# mean forces + run log -> Cd, Re, St per run, summary numbers, and the
# Cd/St vs Re figure and LaTeX table/macros used in the paper
import os

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

L = 0.60  # m, submerged length
TANK_W = 0.90  # m
TANK_H = 0.75  # m, water depth
G = 9.81
MASKELL_M = 2.5  # empirical blockage factor for the Maskell-type correction

# Fixed cylinder -> color/marker, ordered by diameter (validated palette)
STYLE = {
    "1in": ("#2a78d6", "o"),
    "1.5in": ("#eb6834", "s"),
    "2in": ("#1baf7a", "^"),
}
LABEL = {"1in": "$D$ = 25.4 mm", "1.5in": "$D$ = 38.1 mm", "2in": "$D$ = 50.8 mm"}


def water_density(T):
    """kg/m^3, Tanaka et al. (2001), T in deg C."""
    a1, a2, a3, a4, a5 = -3.983035, 301.797, 522528.9, 69.34881, 999.974950
    return a5 * (1 - (T + a1) ** 2 * (T + a2) / (a3 * (T + a4)))


def water_viscosity(T):
    """Pa s, Vogel-type correlation, T in deg C."""
    return 2.414e-5 * 10 ** (247.8 / (T + 273.15 - 140.0))


f = pd.read_csv("processed/forces.csv")
log = pd.read_csv("data/run_log.csv")
df = f.merge(log, left_on="run", right_on="run_id")

D = df.diameter_mm / 1000
U = df.speed_m_s
df["rho"] = water_density(df.water_temp_c)
df["nu"] = water_viscosity(df.water_temp_c) / df.rho
df["Re"] = U * D / df.nu
df["Re_20C"] = U * D / 1.004e-6  # as in the original notebook, for comparison
q_A = 0.5 * df.rho * U**2 * D * L
df["Cd"] = df.F_mean / q_A
# random (block-averaged) + calibration slope uncertainty, added in quadrature
df["Cd_unc"] = df.Cd * np.sqrt(
    (df.F_mean_unc / df.F_mean) ** 2 + (df.sens_std_err / df.sens_V_per_N) ** 2
)
# drag fluctuates at twice the shedding frequency
df["St"] = df.f_peak_Hz / 2 * D / U
df["Fr"] = U / np.sqrt(G * D)
df["LD"] = L / D
df["blockage"] = D * L / (TANK_W * TANK_H)
df["Cd_corr"] = df.Cd / (1 + MASKELL_M * df.Cd * df.blockage)

cols = ["run", "cylinder", "diameter_mm", "speed_m_s", "water_temp_c", "rho", "nu",

# --- Figure: Cd and St vs Re ---
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 9, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(4.5, 5.0), sharex=True,

ax_cd, ax_st = axes

\begin{abstract}
We report towing-tank measurements of the mean drag and vortex-shedding
frequency of smooth, vertical, surface-piercing circular cylinders of
diameter 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8~mm, towed at 0.2--1.1~m/s over
$\mathrm{Re} = \ReMin$--$\ReMax$. Forces were measured with a single in-line
load cell, and each of the \NRuns{} runs was screened by comparing the
load-cell zero before and after the tow. One run with a \ExclDrift~N zero shift was
excluded. Across the remaining \NGood{} runs the drag coefficient based on
the submerged frontal area is $C_D = \CdMean \pm \CdSD$ (mean $\pm$ standard
deviation), with no significant dependence on diameter and a weak increase with
Reynolds number of \CdSlope{} per decade. The Strouhal number inferred from
the drag fluctuation is $\mathrm{St} = \StMean$, constant to within
$\pm\StDev$ over the full range. Run-to-run scatter (about 3\%) is two to
three times the within-run statistical uncertainty, and
blockage corrections reduce the mean to $C_D \approx \CdCorrMean$.
We discuss the roles of blockage, aspect ratio and the free surface in
interpreting these values. \todo{Tighten once the target journal and main message are fixed.}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Flow past a circular cylinder is the canonical bluff-body problem, and its
mean drag and shedding frequency in the subcritical regime are among the
most frequently cited reference data in fluid mechanics
\citep{Zdravkovich1997,Williamson1996}. For a nominally two-dimensional
cylinder at $\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^4$, the drag coefficient lies near
$C_D \approx 1.0$--$1.2$ and the Strouhal number near
$\mathrm{St} \approx 0.2$ \citep{Zdravkovich1997,Norberg2003}.
Measurements in practical facilities, however, depart from the
two-dimensional ideal in several ways: the model spans only part of the
test section and so has a finite aspect ratio; the model and its wake block
part of the cross-section; and in a towing tank the cylinder usually
pierces a free surface \citep{West1982,ChaplinTeigen2003}.

113	For each run the load-cell zero (tare) was taken as the mean voltage over
114	the first second, with the carriage at rest. Force was obtained as
115	$F(t) = [V(t) - V_0]/s$, where $s$ is the calibration sensitivity in effect
116	on the test date. The mean drag $\overline{F}$ was averaged over
117	$3 < t < 8$~s, which lies within the constant-speed portion of every tow.

129	\paragraph{Fluid properties.}
130	Density and kinematic viscosity were evaluated at the measured temperature
131	of each run, using the formulation of \citet{Tanaka2001} for density and a
132	Vogel-type correlation for dynamic viscosity,
133	$\mu = 2.414\times10^{-5}\,10^{247.8/(T-140)}$~Pa\,s with $T$ in kelvin.
134	This agrees with the IAPWS formulation \citep{Huber2009} to within

**Reviewer 1.1 – Reynolds number at the measured temperature.** Already done.
- `analyze.py` calculates density and viscosity from each run's logged `water_temp_c`; the paper describes this in the "Fluid properties" paragraph (`paper/paper.tex:129`).

**Reviewer 1.2 – Run 17.** Already excluded, and the paper says so and gives the reason.
- `process.py` flags runs whose zero shifts by more than 0.05 N between before and after the tow. Run 17 shifted by 4.2 N; no other run shifted by more than 3 mN.

- The figure shows it as an open symbol and the table counts N = 9 for the 50.8 mm cylinder. The stated effects check out: C_D of 1.36 is 18% above the neighbouring runs, and including it would raise that cylinder's mean by about 0.02.

The reviewers were probably looking at an earlier version. Your notes from 2025-11-10 still have the older notebook figures (C_D of 1.18 for the 2 in cylinder), which date from before both of these fixes.

Your draft also still has a few red TODO markers, including one asking you to repeat run 17. Those weren't part of the review, so I left them.
